extracted.intended_audience: people searching for or submitting integer sequences to the OEIS (mathematicians, students, hobbyists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for looking up integer/whole-number sequences in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences and for preparing sequences for submission. Covers how to format queries, clean sequences, use prefixes/wildcards, interpret results, and next steps if no match is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main uses of the OEIS
rubrics_metrics.description: The main uses for the OEIS are: to identify a sequence; to obtain more terms, formulas, references, links, programs, etc. for a sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the OEIS to see if a sequence has been encountered before and to find supporting information (terms, formulas, references, programs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enter about six terms, starting with the second term
rubrics_metrics.description: Enter about 6 terms, starting with the second term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave off the first term or two because people may disagree about where the sequence begins. Example: for 1,1,2,4,9,21,51,127 enter 2,4,9,21,51,127 and leave off the two 1's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit ambiguous initial 0s and 1s
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are several 0's and 1's at the start, leave them off too when you are checking to see if your sequence is already in the OEIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If initial terms are not distinctive (e.g., many 0s or 1s), drop them to improve matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't enter too many terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't enter too many terms, because you may have more terms than are in the OEIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entering an excessive number of terms can prevent matches if the OEIS entry has fewer listed terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean up obvious regularities (omit redundant zeros)
rubrics_metrics.description: If every other term is zero (e.g. 1 0 2 0 4 0 8 0 ...), omit these zeros, and look up 1 2 4 8 16 ... instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform obvious periodic zero patterns or other redundant structure before searching so the canonical sequence is matched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide out common factors before searching
rubrics_metrics.description: If your sequence has an obvious common factor (e.g. 2 6 12 20 30 42 ...), try dividing it out and look up 1 3 6 10 15 21 instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid submitting or searching for a sequence that is just a small integer multiple of an existing sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not submit sequences that are small constants times existing sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, do not submit a sequence which is a small constant times an existing sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to submission, check whether your sequence is just a scalar multiple of a known sequence and refrain from redundant entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search input: numbers, words, or phrases separated appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: The search text is a list of space-separated search terms. The search terms can be single numbers, sequences of numbers, words or strings of words. Sequences of numbers should be separated with commas. Strings of words should be separated by spaces (NOT commas). Strings of words may be enclosed in double quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commas between consecutive numeric terms to indicate order; use spaces and quotes for word phrases. Example: 1,4,9,16 or "fermat's little theorem".

rubrics_metrics.name: Spaces-only numeric queries are auto-comma-inserted for 3+ numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The space-only form is used so often that any time three or more numbers appear in a query separated by spaces, the server inserts commas between them automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may type '1 4 9 16' and it will be treated the same as '1,4,9,16'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas vs quoted numbers: consecutive order vs any order
rubrics_metrics.description: Comma-separated or space-separated numeric lists match numbers appearing consecutively in the given order. To match sequences containing those numbers in any order, the numbers must be individually quoted, e.g. "1" "4" "9" ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unquoted lists enforce order; quoting individual numbers finds entries that contain the numbers anywhere (not necessarily consecutively).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use # prefix to search for numbers anywhere in the entry
rubrics_metrics.description: To search for numbers anywhere in the sequence entry (data, comments, examples etc.), precede the number with a # character and it will be treated as a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '#1759' or '#1957' to find those numbers in any field of an entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes restrict search to particular fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefixes restrict the search to particular lines, e.g.: id:, ref:, program:, seq:, link:, xref:, signed:, formula:, keyword:, name:, example:, author:, offset:, maple:, extension:, comment:, mathematica:, signed:, formula:, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefix:value limits matches to that field. Example: author:LeBrun or keyword:nice. The prefixes mostly correspond to the lines in the display.

rubrics_metrics.name: id: and direct A-number retrieval
rubrics_metrics.description: id:A001006 displays sequence A001006. Typing an A-number (with the A) retrieves the sequence directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can retrieve a known A-number by typing it directly; searching an A-number alone returns that sequence and sequences that mention it.

rubrics_metrics.name: seq: vs signed: prefix behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: seq: matches the sequence data, possibly by ignoring signs. signed: matches sequence data and requires that any signs match as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use signed: when sign pattern matters (example given for the Möbius function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion operators for prefixes and numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a minus sign in front of a prefix to exclude those matches. Put a tilde (~) in front of a number to exclude it (only applies if the numbers are separated by spaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: -seq:5 excludes sequences containing 5. Searching '2 4 ~8 16' returns sequences that do not contain 8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using prefix: by itself to find entries that have that field
rubrics_metrics.description: You can say prefix: by itself to match sequences that have a line of that type. For example ref: will match all sequences with reference lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searching for a bare prefix finds entries that include that line type regardless of its content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequence search: subseq: and signedsubseq:
rubrics_metrics.description: Two prefixes are concerned with subsequences: subseq: and signedsubseq:. You can say, for example, subseq:377,8 to get those numbers in sequence data in that order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these when you are searching for numbers that occur as a (possibly nonconsecutive) subsequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance ordering and scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Results are returned in order of 'relevance,' which orders first by how well the sequence matched the search terms, second by the popularity of the sequence in other sequences' cross-references, and finally by sequence number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Query score details: you get 100 points for matching ordering (having numbers in the same relative order), 10 points for matching terms in certain lines (sequence data counts more, sequence number counts a lot more). Other sort orders are available on the results page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wildcards: _ and __
rubrics_metrics.description: The wildcard _ will match any number in a sequence (as in 1,2,_,4,5). The wildcard __ will match any list of numbers in a sequence (as in 1,2,__,7,8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use _ for a single unknown entry and __ for an arbitrary subsequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search terms highlighted in results
rubrics_metrics.description: Search terms are highlighted in the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matched terms in the entry display are emphasized to help you see why a result matched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation is not indexed
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation is not indexed and is treated as identical to whitespace during matching; for example, searching for fermat's is the same as searching for "fermat s".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on punctuation in queries; treat punctuation as separators or spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma handling with author/book names (no comma in phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The search string Stanley, Combinatorics (with the comma) gets no hits, but searching for Stanley Combinatorics (without the comma) gets several hundred hits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use commas inside word phrases if you want them treated as a phrase; separate words with spaces or use quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searching for large single numbers: try Google
rubrics_metrics.description: To search for a single large number in the OEIS, try Google, because Google has searched all the .txt files in the OEIS, and so may do a better job than the OEIS search engine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 64th Motzkin number is huge and Google may locate it in the b-file for A001006.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimal constants: search their digit sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: For a decimal constant, such as 3.14159, look up the sequence of digits, as in 3 1 4 1 5 9. The OEIS search engine will convert numbers containing decimal points into digit sequences automatically, so you can type 3.14159 directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The engine treats decimal numbers as digit sequences; you can also type digits separated by spaces or commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only integer/whole-number sequences supported
rubrics_metrics.description: You can only look up a sequence of integers or whole numbers, like 6 or 10 or -3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your sequence uses non-integer values, transform them (see fraction/decimal guidance) before searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling fractional sequences: look up numerators and denominators separately
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a sequence of fractions, look up numerators and denominators separately. Example: for 1/4, 5/8, 13/16, 29/32, ... look up 1,5,13,29,61,125 and 4,8,16,32,64,128 separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separating numerators and denominators may help identify underlying integer sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimal fractions and rounding caution
rubrics_metrics.description: If your sequence has decimal fractions in it (1.4, 5.87, 12.083), the OEIS probably can't help you (though you might try rounding them to the nearest integer, or taking the integer part).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rounding or integer-part extraction as heuristics when decimals are involved, but results may be ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: No letter sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no letter sequences (such as A, B, C, D ...) in the OEIS!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to search for or submit sequences of letters; only numeric sequences are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangles: linearize by rows or diagonals
rubrics_metrics.description: For a triangle of numbers, make it into a sequence by reading across the rows (or look up diagonals). Example given showing how to read rows into a flat sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a canonical flattening (rows, diagonals) when searching or submitting triangular data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square arrays: read antidiagonals (or rows/columns)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a square array, make it into a sequence by reading up (or down) the antidiagonals, or look up rows or columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: read antidiagonals to create a linear sequence suitable for OEIS lookup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Index and internal format for reporting updates
rubrics_metrics.description: To see the sequences in the internal format used in the OEIS, click on the 'internal format' link on the results page. This is useful when reporting updates or corrections. Note that there is also an Index to the OEIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the internal format to prepare precise corrections or submissions and consult the Index for topic-oriented searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: WebCam browsing
rubrics_metrics.description: To browse the OEIS, use the WebCam. This can be set to browse the best sequences, recent additions, sequences needing more terms, or all sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the WebCam to work, Javascript must be turned on; it may not work with some older browsers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date format when searching by date
rubrics_metrics.description: Dates have been standardized in the format Jan 01 2001. The month is one of Jan Feb ... Dec. The day is one of 01 02 ... 31, and there may be a comma after the day: Jan 01 2001 and Jan 01, 2001 are both acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find sequences submitted or updated on a particular day, look up both 'Oct 10 2001' and 'Oct 10, 2000' using the word search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of the little numbers in results (query score and reference count)
rubrics_metrics.description: The small numbers at the right of the blue bar indicate query score (e.g. +30) and the number of sequences referencing the given sequence (e.g. 1086).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Query score reflects how well the sequence matched the query (100 points for matching ordering, 10 points for matching terms in certain lines). The references count indicates popularity; relevance sort uses score then reference count.

rubrics_metrics.name: If no match found, try Superseeker
rubrics_metrics.description: If no match is found for your sequence, try Superseeker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superseeker applies additional analyses and heuristics beyond the standard search to help identify or relate your sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: If sequence not in database and of general interest, submit it
rubrics_metrics.description: If your sequence isn't in the database - and is of general interest - please send it to the OEIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting useful sequences helps others and preserves your name for posterity; follow submission format and style guidelines when contributing.
